title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 12
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A pizza chain guarantees delivery within thirty minutes and reports that 95 per cent of its deliveries meet the guarantee. It advertises this as evidence of superior service.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the advertisement?
options: A. Competing chains do not offer guarantees.
B. The chain refuses orders from addresses it judges too distant, so the measured deliveries exclude the journeys most likely to be slow.
C. Some customers order in advance for a specified time.
D. Delivery riders are paid per delivery.
E. The guarantee does not apply in severe weather.
questions.explanation: The statistic is computed on a filtered set, so it describes the selection rule as much as the service. E limits the guarantee but does not bias the measure in the same systematic way.

questions.prompt: A hospital redesigned its signage after finding that many outpatients arrived late for appointments, and reports that late arrivals have fallen. It concludes that confusion about the building's layout had been the cause.
questions.question: The conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: A. Outpatients now arrive earlier than inpatients.
B. All outpatients can read the new signs.
C. The signage cost less than employing additional staff.
D. The fall in late arrivals was not produced by some other change made at the same time, such as revised appointment reminders.
E. Late arrivals had been rising before the change.
questions.explanation: The inference from a fall to a diagnosed cause requires that nothing else plausibly produced it. C is stronger than needed, since the argument survives a minority who cannot use signs.

questions.prompt: A supermarket found that customers who buy plant-based milk also spend more overall than customers who buy dairy milk, and plans to expand its plant-based range in order to raise average spending.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the plan?
options: A. Plant-based milk has a longer shelf life.
B. Some customers buy both kinds.
C. Plant-based milk is bought disproportionately by higher-income customers, whose spending is higher across every category.
D. The plant-based range is more profitable per litre.
E. Dairy milk sales have been stable for several years.
questions.explanation: Income explains both purchases, so stocking more of the product need not change what anyone spends. D would support expansion on different grounds without rescuing the stated reasoning.

questions.prompt: A district raised teacher salaries and, two years later, its pupils' test scores had improved. The education authority attributes the improvement to the salary increase, on the ground that better pay attracts better teachers.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the attribution?
options: A. Teachers report higher job satisfaction.
B. The district also refurbished several schools.
C. Salaries in neighbouring districts were unchanged.
D. Test scores rose nationally over the same period.
E. The proportion of vacancies filled by experienced applicants rose sharply after the increase, and scores improved most in the schools that made such appointments.
questions.explanation: It supplies the intermediate step the mechanism requires and links it to where the effect appeared. C and E introduce rival explanations.

questions.prompt: Every field in the Brackenmoor estate that was treated with the new pesticide is also bordered by a hedgerow. No field bordered by a hedgerow has shown a decline in pollinator numbers this year. Some fields on the estate have shown a decline in pollinator numbers.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Some fields on the estate were not treated with the new pesticide.
B. The new pesticide is harmless to pollinators.
C. Hedgerows protect pollinators.
D. Most fields on the estate have hedgerows.
E. Fields without hedgerows were treated with a different pesticide.
questions.explanation: Fields with declines exist; such a field has no hedgerow, and treatment implies a hedgerow, so those fields were untreated. B and C draw causal conclusions the statements cannot support.

questions.prompt: A gym replaced half its treadmills with rowing machines after a survey showed that members rated rowing more highly. Six months later, total equipment use had fallen.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in explaining this outcome?
options: A. How much the rowing machines cost
B. Whether the members who rated rowing highly were the same members who accounted for most equipment use
C. Whether the gym advertised the change
D. How many members the gym has
E. Whether rowing machines require more maintenance
questions.explanation: A rating averaged over members says nothing about the intensity of use behind it; if heavy users preferred treadmills, the change removes capacity where demand was concentrated.

questions.prompt: An airport authority argues that a proposed night flight ban is unnecessary, since a survey of residents found that only 12 per cent describe aircraft noise as a serious problem.
questions.question: The argument is most vulnerable to the objection that it
options: A. relies on a survey conducted by the authority itself
B. ignores the economic benefits of night flights
C. does not define what counts as a night flight
D. assumes residents understand aircraft schedules
E. treats the proportion of all residents as the relevant figure, when the burden falls on those living under the flight paths
questions.explanation: Averaging over a population that mostly is not exposed conceals a concentrated harm — the standard defect of area-wide statistics applied to localised effects.

questions.prompt: A hotel chain placed cards in bathrooms asking guests to reuse towels, and reports that laundry volumes fell. It concludes that guests are willing to help reduce environmental impact when asked.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion?
options: A. The chain simultaneously reduced the number of towels placed in each room, and guests who wanted fresh towels had to request them.
B. Some guests stay only one night.
C. The cards were printed on recycled paper.
D. Laundry costs have risen industry-wide.
E. Housekeeping staff were told about the scheme.
questions.explanation: Reducing supply and adding a request step produces the same measured fall through friction rather than willingness, which is what the conclusion claims to have demonstrated.

questions.prompt: A factory that services its machines on a fixed schedule finds that breakdowns cluster in the weeks just before scheduled servicing. The plant manager concludes that servicing should be carried out more frequently.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the manager's conclusion?
options: A. Servicing requires the line to be stopped for a day.
B. Spare parts are held on site.
C. Most breakdowns occur in machines that had been running well past their recommended operating hours, a threshold reached at different times for different machines.
D. Some machines are newer than others.
E. Breakdowns are recorded by shift supervisors.
questions.explanation: If wear is driven by operating hours rather than elapsed calendar time, uniformly more frequent servicing is the wrong remedy — condition-based scheduling is. A is a cost, not a defect in the reasoning.

questions.prompt: A studio observes that its sequels earn more in their opening week than its original films, and concludes that audiences prefer sequels.
questions.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. ignores the cost of producing sequels
B. compares opening-week figures rather than total earnings
C. does not account for inflation in ticket prices
D. overlooks that sequels are made only for films that were already successful, and are marketed to an audience that already exists
E. assumes all sequels are of similar quality
questions.explanation: The population of sequels is selected on prior success, so the comparison is with all originals including the failures — the difference need reflect no preference at all.

questions.prompt: Campaigners argue that a supermarket's loyalty card data should be used to warn customers whose purchases suggest a health risk. A critic replies that purchase records show what a household buys, not what any individual eats.
questions.question: The critic's reply undermines the proposal by
options: A. questioning the legality of using the data
B. identifying a gap between what the data measure and what the inference requires
C. arguing that customers would object to being contacted
D. denying that diet affects health
E. proposing an alternative source of information
questions.explanation: The measurement-to-inference gap is the specific defect: a household basket cannot be attributed to a person, so the warning may reach the wrong one.

questions.passageText:
An insurer sets a premium reflecting the average risk of those it expects to insure. Buyers know more about their own risk than the insurer does, and those who know themselves to be low risk find the average premium poor value and decline it. The pool that remains is riskier than the one the premium was calculated for, so the premium must rise, which drives out the next-safest group. The spiral is the central problem of insurance markets and does not require anyone to lie.

Insurers respond by trying to observe what buyers know. Medical questionnaires, driving records, telematics and waiting periods for pre-existing conditions all serve to sort applicants into narrower classes. The sorting works, and it has a consequence rarely stated by its advocates: perfect sorting would eliminate insurance. A policy priced exactly to an individual's known risk transfers nothing, since the buyer pays what they expect to lose. Insurance exists because of what is not known.

Two devices limit the spiral without abolishing the product. Compulsory purchase forces low risks to remain in the pool, which is why so many insurance markets are mandatory. Group schemes attached to employment achieve something similar, since people take a job for reasons unrelated to their health, and the resulting pool is close to random.

The design question is therefore not whether to interfere with the market but how. An unregulated market unravels from the safe end; a fully pooled one invites the higher risks to buy more cover than they otherwise would. Every real scheme sits somewhere between, and where it sits is a political decision wearing technical clothes.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, the adverse selection spiral begins when
options: A. insurers deliberately misprice policies
B. regulators require insurers to accept all applicants
C. low-risk buyers find the average premium poor value and decline it
D. buyers conceal information from insurers
E. claims exceed the insurer's reserves
questions.explanation: The passage is explicit that the spiral requires no dishonesty: it follows from low risks rationally declining an averaged premium.

questions.passageText:
Dogs were the first domesticated animal, and the details have been unusually resistant to settlement. Ancient DNA has revised the picture repeatedly, and the pattern of those revisions is worth attention.

Two things are now reasonably secure. Dogs descend from a population of wolves that is extinct rather than from any living wolf population, which is why comparisons with modern wolves were misleading for decades. And domestication preceded agriculture: the earliest securely identified dog remains come from hunting societies, which rules out the intuitive account in which wolves were drawn to farming settlements by refuse.

Almost everything else remains contested. Estimates of when domestication began span thousands of years, because the methods disagree: molecular clocks calibrated on mutation rates give older dates than the archaeological record, and identifying a skeleton as dog rather than wolf is difficult precisely at the period of interest, when the two would have been most similar. Whether domestication happened once or several times has been argued in both directions by the same laboratories as new genomes arrived.

The instructive point concerns evidence rather than dogs. Each revision has come from a new class of data rather than from more of the existing kind — ancient genomes rather than modern ones, morphometric analysis rather than eye judgement. Adding further specimens of a type already sampled has generally sharpened confidence intervals without resolving disagreements, which suggests the remaining questions are limited by the kind of evidence available and not by its quantity.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that comparisons between dogs and modern wolves were misleading because
options: A. dogs descend from a wolf population that is now extinct
B. modern wolves have interbred with dogs
C. wolf populations have declined sharply
D. modern wolves live in different habitats
E. the comparisons used too few specimens
questions.explanation: Stated as one of the two secure findings.

questions.passageText:
The case for patents is a bargain: an inventor receives a temporary monopoly, and in exchange discloses how the invention works, so that others may build on it once the term expires. The argument is coherent, and the evidence that the system delivers on it is weaker than its centrality to policy would suggest.

Historical comparisons are the most interesting evidence available. Some industries flourished in periods and places with weak or absent patent protection, and studies of nineteenth-century exhibitions found that inventors in countries without patent laws produced innovations at rates comparable to those in countries with them, though concentrated in different fields. Where imitation is easy and development costs are high — pharmaceuticals is the standard example — the case for protection is strongest; where products are complex and assembled from thousands of components, patents can obstruct the very cumulative development they were meant to encourage.

That obstruction has a name. When a product requires licences from many holders, each can demand a price reflecting its power to block the whole, and the sum of independently set prices exceeds what a single owner would charge. The result is that a product worth making does not get made.

The reasonable conclusion is neither abolition nor expansion. It is that the optimal strength of protection differs by industry in ways a single national system cannot easily reflect, and that the burden of proof for extending terms or broadening what may be patented should sit with those proposing it, which is not where it has generally sat.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that the case for patent protection is strongest where
options: A. products are assembled from thousands of components
B. national systems are uniform across industries
C. inventors work in universities
D. imitation is easy and development costs are high
E. terms of protection are long
questions.explanation: Pharmaceuticals is given as the standard example of exactly those conditions.

questions.passageTitle: How a Writer Enters the Canon
questions.passageText:
Literary reputations are commonly explained by merit, and merit is doing less work in that explanation than it appears to. The books that survive are not simply the best ones; they are the ones that continued to be reprinted, taught and referred to, and those processes have their own logic.

Reprinting requires a publisher expecting sales, which depends on a work being known, which depends on its having been reprinted. The circularity is self-reinforcing in both directions, and a book that falls out of print for a generation faces an obstacle unrelated to its quality. Teaching amplifies this: a work on a syllabus generates criticism, criticism generates scholarly interest, and scholarly interest justifies its place on the syllabus.

The clearest evidence comes from recovery. When scholars deliberately reprinted neglected writers — many of them women publishing in periods when their work was reviewed respectfully and then dropped from later accounts — a substantial number entered general reading and stayed there. That such recoveries succeed indicates the earlier exclusion was not a verdict on quality that later readers simply confirmed.

None of this establishes that judgement is arbitrary. Some works do continue to be read across centuries and languages and remote contexts, and explaining that entirely by institutional momentum is implausible. The defensible position is that survival requires quality and something else besides, that the something else is contingent, and that a canon is therefore evidence about what was transmitted rather than a ranking of what was written.
questions.prompt: The passage suggests that a book falling out of print for a generation
options: A. has usually been judged inferior by readers
B. faces an obstacle unrelated to its quality
C. can be recovered only if its author is still living
D. will be preserved through teaching
E. loses its copyright protection
questions.explanation: The circularity of reprinting and being known operates in both directions, and the obstacle is structural rather than evaluative.

readingPassages.title: How a Writer Enters the Canon
readingPassages.text:
Literary reputations are commonly explained by merit, and merit is doing less work in that explanation than it appears to. The books that survive are not simply the best ones; they are the ones that continued to be reprinted, taught and referred to, and those processes have their own logic.

Reprinting requires a publisher expecting sales, which depends on a work being known, which depends on its having been reprinted. The circularity is self-reinforcing in both directions, and a book that falls out of print for a generation faces an obstacle unrelated to its quality. Teaching amplifies this: a work on a syllabus generates criticism, criticism generates scholarly interest, and scholarly interest justifies its place on the syllabus.

The clearest evidence comes from recovery. When scholars deliberately reprinted neglected writers — many of them women publishing in periods when their work was reviewed respectfully and then dropped from later accounts — a substantial number entered general reading and stayed there. That such recoveries succeed indicates the earlier exclusion was not a verdict on quality that later readers simply confirmed.

None of this establishes that judgement is arbitrary. Some works do continue to be read across centuries and languages and remote contexts, and explaining that entirely by institutional momentum is implausible. The defensible position is that survival requires quality and something else besides, that the something else is contingent, and that a canon is therefore evidence about what was transmitted rather than a ranking of what was written.
